nameStory: The Eastern Waterfan gets its name from its distinctive fan-like shape and its love of water – it's one of the few lichens that actually lives submerged in streams! The 'fan' part comes from how its dark, ruffled edges spread out like an old-fashioned hand fan. It's called 'Eastern' to distinguish it from its western cousins that live in mountain streams across the continent.
description: Eastern Waterfan Lichen is a rare and remarkable aquatic lichen that forms small, dark rosettes in cold mountain streams. Unlike most lichens that avoid water, this species thrives while completely submerged, attaching itself to rocks and bedrock in shaded stream areas. It appears as blackish, fan-shaped patches with distinctively ruffled, wavy edges and prominent vein-like patterns running through its surface. The entire lichen has a somewhat gelatinous, rubbery texture when wet.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Lives completely or partially submerged in cold, clean mountain streams – the only lichen you'll find actually living underwater in New England

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms small, fan-shaped rosettes with distinctly ruffled, wavy margins that flutter in the current like underwater lettuce leaves

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Appears blackish to dark brown when submerged, with prominent lighter veining that creates a roadmap-like pattern across the surface

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Feels distinctly gelatinous and rubbery when wet, almost like touching a piece of wet seaweed or kelp

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always attached to rocks, bedrock, or large stones in flowing water, never on soil or tree bark like other pelt lichens

habitat: Look for Eastern Waterfan Lichen in cold, clean mountain streams throughout New England's higher elevations, particularly in shaded areas where the water flows over rocks and bedrock. It prefers pristine riparian environments with good water quality and consistent flow. You'll find it attached to submerged or semi-submerged stones in areas protected from direct sunlight by overhanging trees or steep stream banks.

seasonality.spring: Most visible during spring snowmelt when streams are running high and clear, though the lichen may be harder to spot due to increased water flow and debris.
seasonality.summer: Easier to observe during lower water levels in late summer when rocks become partially exposed, revealing the dark rosettes clinging to stone surfaces.
seasonality.fall: Good viewing continues through fall as water levels remain manageable and fallen leaves provide contrast against the dark lichen on rocks.
seasonality.winter: May be visible under ice in shallow areas, appearing as dark spots frozen beneath the surface, though access is often difficult due to winter conditions.

funFact: This lichen can actually photosynthesize while completely underwater – it's like a tiny underwater solar panel that can live its entire life submerged in mountain streams, something almost no other lichen on Earth can do!
confusionNotes: The only real confusion might be with dark algae or small aquatic plants, but Eastern Waterfan's distinctive fan shape with ruffled edges and prominent veining pattern sets it apart from any slimy stream algae. Remember: if it's fan-shaped with wavy edges and living on rocks in a stream, it's likely this rare lichen.
contextualKnowledge: This species was originally placed in its own genus called Hydrothyria (meaning 'water door') because scientists couldn't believe a true lichen could live underwater. Only DNA studies in 2000 proved it was actually a highly specialized member of the pelt lichen family that evolved to conquer an entirely new habitat.
compareHints: Unlike all other pelt lichens in New England, Eastern Waterfan is the only one that lives in water rather than on soil, rocks, or trees in terrestrial habitats. While other pelt lichens like Dog Pelt or Freckled Pelt form larger, leaf-like lobes on land, Eastern Waterfan creates small, ruffled rosettes with a gelatinous texture adapted for stream life. Its closest relatives are found in western North America's mountain streams, not in New England's forests.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the pelt lichens, scaly pelt is the only one in New England with prominent phyllidia scattered across its surface.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, horizontal pelt lichen is unique for its completely prostrate growth habit - it never curls up at the edges like dog pelt lichen or forms the ruffled, frilly margins of freckled pelt lichen.
Distinguished from dog pelt lichen by having many more fruiting structures along the edges rather than just a few large ones.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, dog pelt lichen stands out for its preference for growing directly on soil rather than trees, and its particularly well-defined dark veining on a pale underside.
Among the pelt lichens, ruffled freckled pelt stands out for its notably bumpy, textured surface and strongly ruffled edges.
Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has evenly-spaced, rounded lobes, alternating dog lichen has its distinctive alternating finger-like projections along the edges.
Among the pelt lichens, freckled pelt is the only one with distinctive dark green cephalodia (freckles), making identification fairly straightforward.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a smooth surface, peppered pelt is distinguished by its dark spotted pattern.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, sheepish pelt lichen is distinguished by its uniquely woolly surface texture - most other Peltigera species have smooth or slightly wrinkled surfaces.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a relatively uniform surface with veins on the underside, concentric pelt lichen displays obvious ring patterns on top.
